title: zebra-cover: Let the Model Read the Puzzle, Let Knuth Solve It
author: Tatra Labs

sections.value: Language models are bad at Zebra puzzles (the Swede keeps a dog, the green house is directly left of the white one) because solving one is a long search with backtracking, and a model writing left to right cannot take a move back. Exact cover is a problem shape made for exactly that search, and Donald Knuth's dancing-links algorithms solve it in milliseconds.

From Natural Language to Exact Cover (Skaisgiris, Pammer, Semmelrock, Ielanskyi, Heisinger and Kobler; TU Wien, JKU Linz and the University of Klagenfurt; November 2026) splits the work between the two. The model only translates: it reads the puzzle and writes tool calls, one per clue. A solver finds every grid consistent with those calls, and its verdict goes back to the model. With Qwen3-30B-Instruct the paper solves 95% of ZebraLogic puzzles this way, against 70.9% when the same model answers directly, and with Devstral Small 2 it reaches 97.9%, above the best entry on the public leaderboard. Its code runs on vLLM and a GPU.
zebra-cover is the same loop in 1,012 lines of standard-library Python with no dependencies: Knuth's Algorithm C, a generator of fresh puzzles that have exactly one solution, each with its gold tool calls, the paper's tools behind a strict checker, the feedback loop, a grader, and backends for a local transformers model or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

```bash
pip install -e .
zebra-cover generate --size 4x4 --seed 3   # one puzzle, one answer
zebra-cover gold --size 5x5 --seed 0       # encode, solve, print
```

The solver is never the bottleneck. On gold encodings its median time is 3.6 ms for a 4×4 puzzle, 14 ms at 5×5 and 78 ms at 6×6, in pure Python. A clue like "next to" becomes one item with one option per pair of houses it allows, and Algorithm C's colours let several options share a cell as long as they agree on what is in it. Its 44 tests run in four seconds.
## What two small models do with it

The paper's headline results come from models of 20 to 30 billion parameters. I had a CPU and the two Qwen3 models already on the machine, 0.6B and 1.7B, so this is a small test: 30 fresh puzzles, five at each of six sizes from 2 houses × 3 attributes up to 5 × 5, greedy decoding, thinking off. One feedback run on 1.7B took between 3 and 76 minutes per puzzle. Treat it as evidence about how the method fails, not as a leaderboard.

| Qwen3-1.7B, 30 puzzles | solved | cells right |
|---|---:|---:|
| answer directly | **4** | 43.7% |
| tool calls + solver, one shot | 1 | 3.3% |
| tool calls + solver + feedback, 4 rounds | 1 | 5.6% |
| the one-shot replies, lenient reader | **7** | 28.8% |

Qwen3-0.6B solved none by any method: 30.6% of cells right when it answered directly, and not one tool call that could be checked.
As specified, the method loses to plain answering at this scale. The strict loop solves 1 puzzle of 30; answering directly solves 4, all of them the smallest size. Feedback did not help: 1.7B solved nothing more in rounds two to four.

Most of the gap is spelling, not reasoning. Score each first-round clue call from 1.7B against the gold call for that clue, by meaning, so that left-of(A, B) and right-of(B, A) match: 54% are right as written, and 80% once near-miss tool names are mapped to the closest real one. The model writes `clue_property_right_of_property` for `clue_property_right_of`, 144 times across its replies, and `clue_property_property` for `clue_property_at_property`. Only 5 wrong calls are the left-right swap you might expect from a small model. But one unknown name invalidates a whole reply, and 24 of the 30 first replies were rejected outright.

Read those same replies with the aliases and 7 puzzles of 30 are solved, six of them at sizes from 3×3 to 4×5, where plain answering solves none. That number is exact for a one-shot run with a lenient reader, because a first reply never depends on feedback. But the alias table was written after seeing the replies, so it is a diagnosis rather than a result, and the strict reader stays the default.

Feedback broke on bookkeeping. In 12 of 82 later-round replies, 1.7B re-sent its clue calls but dropped `init_zebra`, so nothing could be encoded at all; 0.6B dropped it in 78 of 90. The invented tool names kept coming back after the error message had listed the valid ones. And a unique solution can still be wrong: four encodings from 1.7B had exactly one solution, two of them first replies and two reached through feedback, and only one was the right grid. The solver can check that the calls agree with each other. It cannot check that they say what the clues say.
## What the paper says about small models

None of this contradicts the paper, and part of it is in the paper. Its Appendix C runs the same comparison across Qwen3 sizes on ZebraLogic, and at the two sizes I could run, answering directly wins there too.

The crossover sits between 1.7B and 4B parameters. Above it, translation is the easy half and the solver does the rest; below it, the model cannot yet use the tools reliably. My puzzles are generated in the ZebraLogic style rather than taken from ZebraLogic, so the two sets of numbers agree in direction, not cell for cell.

One engineering finding worth passing on: handing the tools to Qwen3 through its chat template's tool slot makes the model stop after its first call and wait for a result. The paper's format is a single reply containing every call, so the tool schemas go into the system prompt as plain text.

What this is not: a reproduction of the paper's numbers. It runs no 20B or 30B model, uses neither ZebraLogic nor the paper's ZebraExtreme set, and replaces the paper's MiniExact solver with a from-scratch Algorithm C that solves the same encoding. The method is Skaisgiris and colleagues'. What this adds is the loop with nothing to install, a puzzle generator with gold calls, and every reply from both models stored in the repository, so each number above can be recomputed without running a model. Pointing it at a larger model is one command against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and nothing here has done that yet.
